claim: Sensory neurons adapt their response threshold and gain to the range of inputs that they recently received.
source: Seminal work by Barlow (1961) and Laughlin (1981) demonstrated that sensory neurons in early processing stages adapt their response threshold and gain to the range of inputs that they recently received.
evidence: Supported by citations to Barlow (1961) and Laughlin (1981)

claim: Gain adaptation has been shown in the fly H1 neuron.
source: A particularly striking example of such gain modulation at the single cell level has been shown in the fly H1 neuron (Brenner et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brenner et al., 2000

claim: Gain adaptation has been observed in early sensory circuits including the retina and auditory hair cells.
source: Gain adaptation has been observed in other early sensory circuits (Blakemore and Campbell, 1969; Fairhall et al., 2001; Solomon and Kohn, 2014; Wark et al., 2007), such as in the retina (Kastner and Baccus, 2014), auditory hair cells (Nagel and Doupe, 2006; Wen et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: Adaptation is present in later sensory stages.
source: and is also present in later sensory stages (Adibi et al., 2013; Wainwright, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adibi et al., 2013 and Wainwright, 1999

claim: Cortical neurons acquire adaptation properties during development.
source: Moreover, cortical neurons acquire this property during development (Mease et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mease et al., 2013

claim: Neural adaptation maximizes information transfer.
source: The work of Laughlin and Barlow was instrumental in uncovering a principle of neural adaption as maximizing information transfer.
evidence: Based on established work by Laughlin and Barlow

claim: Changes in neural gains may result in profound changes of the mapping of neural responses to stimuli in a history-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, such changes in neural gains may result in profound changes of the mapping of neural responses to stimuli in a history-dependent manner.
evidence: Logical inference from the discussion of adaptation effects

claim: Adaptation has been interpreted as the source of perceptual illusions such as the tilt after-effect or the waterfall illusion.
source: This has been interpreted as the source of perceptual illusions such as the tilt after-effect or the waterfall illusion (Barlow and Hill, 1963; Wainwright, 1999; Clifford, 2014; He and MacLeod, 2001; Schwartz et al., 2009).

claim: Adaptation affects neural responses even at short time scales or after only one repetition of the same stimulus.
source: However, adaptation deeply affects neural responses even at short time scales or after only one repetition of the same stimulus (Patterson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patterson et al., 2013

claim: A random recurrent network with spike-based adaptation produces highly inaccurate decoding of visual patterns.
source: When subjected to this spike-time dependent adaptation, the responses became strongly history dependent, resulting in a highly inaccurate decoding (Figure 1b, 3rd row).
evidence: Demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 1b, 3rd row

claim: Recurrent connections can be tuned such that spike-dependent adaptation will not impair the stability of the representation.
source: In this study, we show that this is not necessarily the case. Recurrent connections can be tuned such that spike-dependent adaptation will not impair the stability of the representation (Figure 1b, bottom row).
evidence: Demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 1b, bottom row

claim: Spike-frequency adaptation and E/I balanced recurrent connectivity emerge as solutions to a global cost-accuracy tradeoff.
source: We show that spike-frequency adaptation and E/I balanced recurrent connectivity emerge as solutions to a global cost-accuracy tradeoff.
evidence: Main theoretical result derived from the model

claim: The network will redistribute sensory responses from highly excitable neurons to less excitable neurons as the cost of neural activity increases.
source: The network will redistribute sensory responses from highly excitable neurons to less excitable neurons as the cost of neural activity increases.

claim: Redistribution of activity does not change the representation at the population level despite causing dynamic changes in individual neurons.
source: This does not change the representation at the population level despite causing dynamic changes in individual neurons.

claim: Spiking comes with inherent metabolic costs for biological neurons.
source: For biological neurons, spiking comes with inherent metabolic costs.

claim: Resources are expended after each spike and neurons or neural populations may need some time to recover from a period of strong activity.
source: For example, resources are expended after each spike and neurons or neural populations may need some time to recover from a period of strong activity.

claim: The dynamics allowing metabolic resources to be replenished are slower than the time scale at which neural populations transmit information.
source: The underlying assumption is that the dynamics allowing metabolic resources to be replenished are slower than the time scale at which neural populations transmit information.

claim: A neuron spikes only when doing so reduces the decoding error.
source: Our framework revolves around the assumption that a neuron spikes only when doing so reduces the decoding error.
evidence: Core assumption of the theoretical framework

claim: Neurons are connected by mutually inhibitory synapses determined by their decoding weights.
source: Neurons are connected by mutually inhibitory synapses determined by their decoding weights.

claim: Spike-frequency adaptation in single neurons is part of the solution to the cost-accuracy tradeoff.
source: This indicates that spike-frequency adaptation in single neurons is part of the solution to the cost-accuracy tradeoff.

claim: Spike-frequency adaptation cannot work alone and needs to be associated with appropriately tuned recurrent connections.
source: However, we will show that it cannot work alone; it needs to be associated with appropriately tuned recurrent connections.
evidence: Prediction from the theoretical model to be demonstrated

claim: Neurons with the smallest decoding weights tend to respond most strongly to the stimulus.
source: As a result, neurons with the smallest decoding weights (and thus, the highest precision in representing the input) tend to respond most strongly to the stimulus (Figure 2a).
evidence: Derived from the model and illustrated in Figure 2a

claim: Neurons with large decoding weights and small input weights bring less precision to the estimate but are metabolically efficient.
source: In contrast, neurons with large decoding weights and small input weights (thus 'low gain' neurons) bring less precision to the estimate but are metabolically efficient.
evidence: Logical inference from the model structure

claim: If μ=0, only the most excitable neuron will respond to the stimulus while completely inhibiting the other neurons.
source: Thus, it will always favor precision over cost. In that case, only the most excitable neuron (with the smallest decoding weight) will respond to the stimulus while completely inhibiting the other neurons.
evidence: Prediction from the mathematical model when cost parameter is zero

claim: Model neurons in isolation respond to a step-like input with a rate that decreases exponentially in time before reaching a plateau.
source: Model neurons in isolation (i.e. without any contribution from recurrent connections) would respond to a step-like input with a rate that decreases exponentially in time before reaching a plateau (Figure 2c)
evidence: Demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 2c

claim: Highly excitable neurons adapt strongly, while less excitable neurons adapt weakly.
source: Highly excitable neurons adapt strongly, while less excitable neurons adapt weakly.

claim: During sustained stimulation, the response of each neuron fluctuates dynamically despite the fact that the stimulus is constant.
source: During sustained stimulation, the response of each neuron fluctuates dynamically despite the fact that the stimulus is constant (Figure 3b).
evidence: Demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 3b

claim: Without recurrent connections, the population response wanders from the iso-coding line.
source: However, if one removes the recurrent connections and plots the response of one neuron as a function of the other (Figure 3c, right), we discover that the population response wanders from the iso-coding line
evidence: Demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 3c, right

claim: The intact network with recurrent connections coordinates the two neurons such that the weighted sum of their responses remains accurate.
source: In contrast, the intact network with its recurrent connections coordinates the two neurons such that the weighted sum of their responses remains accurate.

claim: The movement of activity along the manifold reflects a progressive redistribution of activity to satisfy the unfolding cost-accuracy tradeoff.
source: The movement of the activity along the manifold defined by the constant stimulus and the decoding weights reflects a progressive redistribution of activity to satisfy the unfolding cost-accuracy tradeoff, as the cost slowly accumulates (Figure 3d).
evidence: Interpretation of simulation results shown in Figure 3d

claim: Both high gain and low gain neurons contribute to population adaptation by coordinating and adapting their activity.
source: in fact both contribute to population adaptation because both neurons coordinate and adapt their activity to limit the metabolic cost of the representation while maintaining its accuracy.

claim: Recurrent connections deeply affect the dynamics of each neuron.
source: Recurrent connections deeply affect the dynamics of each neuron.

claim: The inhibition from the strongly excitable neuron is responsible for the response delay of the weakly excitable neuron.
source: For example, the inhibition from the strongly excitable neuron is responsible for the response delay of the weakly excitable neuron.

claim: The first neurons to be recruited are strongly excitable and provide an initially very precise representation of the signal.
source: The first neurons to be recruited are strongly excitable and provide an initially very precise representation of the signal.

claim: Strongly excitable neurons inhibit the less excitable neurons, preventing them from firing early in the stimulation period.
source: These neurons inhibit the less excitable neurons, preventing them from firing early in this stimulation period.

claim: As the cost accumulates, the response of high gain neurons decays due to spike-frequency adaptation.
source: As the cost accumulates, however, the response of the high gain neurons decays due to spike-frequency adaptation.

claim: Weakly excitable neurons become disinhibited, fire, and then adapt in their turn.
source: This is compensated by weakly excitable neurons that become disinhibited, fire, and then adapt in their turn.

claim: The less excitable a neuron is, the later it will be recruited, resulting in strong response delays.
source: The less excitable a neuron is, the later it will be recruited, resulting in strong response delays.

claim: The dynamic response properties of individual neurons are dominated by network interactions and are markedly different from their intrinsic adaptive properties.
source: The dynamic response properties of individual neurons are thus dominated by network interactions and are markedly different from their intrinsic adaptive properties (Figure 2).
evidence: Comparison between isolated neuron behavior (Figure 2) and network behavior

claim: The disinhibition of weakly excitable neurons automatically compensates for the decay in strongly excitable neural responses.
source: Because the disinhibition of weakly excitable neurons automatically compensates for the decay in strongly excitable neural responses, the stimulus representation remains stable during the whole period (Figure 4d).
evidence: Demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 4d

claim: The precision of the representation degrades as more low gain neurons contribute to the representation.
source: However, note that its precision degrades as more low gain neurons contribute to the representation.

claim: The bias and standard deviation of the representation increases as imposed by the global cost/accuracy tradeoff.
source: As a result, the bias and standard deviation of the representation increases as imposed by the global cost/accuracy tradeoff.

claim: The lateral connections derived from the model maximally inhibit neurons with similar preferred orientations and excite neurons with orthogonal orientations.
source: The lateral connections derived from the model maximally inhibit neurons with similar preferred orientations and excite neurons with orthogonal orientations (see schematic in Figure 5a)
evidence: Derived from the model structure and illustrated in Figure 5a

claim: High gain neurons respond first, then adapt during prolonged oriented stimulus presentation.
source: As seen in the simpler model from Figure 4, high gain neurons respond first, then adapt.

claim: As the responses of strongly excitable neurons decay, weakly excitable neurons are recruited, maintaining the representation.
source: As the responses of those strongly excitable neurons decay, weakly excitable neurons are recruited, maintaining the representation.

claim: Highly excitable neurons are suppressed relative to their early responses after adaptation.
source: Highly excitable neurons are suppressed relative to their early responses (Figure 6, top).
evidence: Demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 6, top

claim: Weakly excitable neurons see their tuning curves widen when the adapting stimulus is similar to their preferred orientation.
source: In contrast, weakly excitable neurons see their tuning curves widen when the adapting stimulus is similar to their preferred orientation (Figure 6, bottom).
evidence: Demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 6, bottom

claim: At the flank of the adapting orientation, low gain neurons see an increase in their responsiveness.
source: At the flank of the adapting orientation, low gain neurons see an increase in their responsiveness.

claim: The disinhibition from strongly excitable neurons combined with constant feedforward drive results in facilitated activity in weakly excitable neurons rather than suppressed activity.
source: In other words, the disinhibition from strongly excitable neurons combined with the constant feedforward drive to these low gain neurons results in facilitated activity rather than the suppressed activity one would expect to be caused by adaptation.

claim: The tuning curves for the most excitable neurons are broader than those for weakly excitable neurons.
source: Finally, the tuning curves for the most excitable neurons are broader than those for weakly excitable neurons.

claim: Tuning curves can be either facilitated or suppressed by adaptation in a network with random distribution of preferred orientations and decoding weights.
source: Tuning curves can be either facilitated or suppressed by adaptation.
evidence: Observation from simulation results with random network

claim: When the adapted stimulus falls on the flank of the tuning curve, it can be accompanied by a shift toward or away from the adapting stimulus.
source: When the adapted stimulus falls on the flank of the tuning curve, it can be accompanied by a shift toward or away from the adapting stimulus.

claim: The effect of adaptation on single neurons is variable due to local heterogeneity in the competition they receive from other neurons.
source: The effect of adaptation on single neurons is variable not because of noise (we did not introduce any) but because of local heterogeneity in the competition they receive from other neurons, itself due to the random choices of weights.

claim: Adaptation in one neuron would be impossible to predict quantitatively without observing the rest of the network.
source: In fact, adaptation in one neuron would be impossible to predict quantitatively without observing the rest of the network.

claim: The network is designed to negotiate the tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency.
source: The network is designed to negotiate the tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency and it will prioritize the production of a stable representation if µ is small.

claim: If µ is large, the network will favor cost over accuracy.
source: If µ is large, the network will favor cost over accuracy.

claim: Strong adaptation and prolonged stimulus presentation can produce a representation that degrades over time.
source: Thus, strong adaptation and a prolonged stimulus presentation can produce a representation that degrades over time.

claim: The model replicates the tilt illusion effect.
source: Our model replicates this effect (Figure 8c,d).
evidence: Demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 8c,d

claim: Test stimuli within a range of 0–45 degrees difference from the adaptor orientation are repulsed whereas test stimuli with greater than 45 degree difference are attracted.
source: Test stimuli within a range of 0–45 degrees difference from the adaptor orientation are repulsed whereas test stimuli with a greater than 45 degree difference from the adaptor orientation are attracted (Figure 8d).
evidence: Demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 8d

claim: The repulsion effect has a greater amplitude than the attraction effect.
source: In accordance with experimental findings, the repulsion effect has a greater amplitude than the attraction effect.
evidence: Observation from simulation results compared to experimental findings

claim: Sensory neurons in cortex are embedded in highly recurrent networks with each cell receiving strong inhibitory currents that co-vary with excitatory currents.
source: Sensory neurons in cortex are embedded in highly recurrent networks with each cell receiving strong inhibitory currents that co-vary with excitatory currents (Graupner and Reyes, 2013) and are thus E/I balanced.
evidence: Supported by citation to Graupner and Reyes, 2013

claim: In balanced networks, heterogeneous sensory neurons with activity dependent suppression solve a global cost/accuracy tradeoff rather than a local tradeoff at the level of each neuron.
source: Here, we show that in balanced networks, heterogeneous sensory neurons with activity dependent suppression solve a global cost/accuracy tradeoff rather than a local tradeoff at the level of each neuron.
evidence: Main conclusion from the theoretical model

claim: Adaptation at the level of individual neurons co-exists with a largely stable representation at the population level.
source: In our case, adaptation at the level of individual neurons co-exists with a largely stable representation at the population level.

claim: E/I balance indirectly ensures that neural activity is redistributed from highly responsive neurons to less responsive neurons without changing the interpretation by downstream areas.
source: Rather than being globally suppressed by adaptation, E/I balance indirectly ensures that the neural activity is redistributed from highly responsive neurons to less responsive neurons without changing the interpretation of this activity by downstream areas.

claim: Given adaptation, neural coding cannot be understood at the level of a single neuron, except in cases where a unique sensory feature is solely encoded by a single neuron.
source: Our approach suggests that, given adaptation, neural coding cannot be understood at the level of a single neuron, except in cases where a unique sensory feature is solely encoded by a single neuron, such as the H1 neuron (Brenner et al., 2000).
evidence: Conclusion from the model with citation to example

claim: In areas containing large numbers of interconnected neurons with redundant selectivity, many questions about neural coding and adaptation are only meaningful when applied to whole populations.
source: In areas containing large numbers of interconnected neurons with redundant selectivity, many questions about neural coding and adaptation are only meaningful when applied to whole populations.

claim: The adapting tuning curves of a single neuron can reflect a collective, flexible solution found by the network in particular contexts.
source: We show that the adapting tuning curves of a single neuron can reflect a collective, flexible solution found by the network in particular contexts.

claim: Other studies have used predictive coding and efficient coding frameworks to construct models of adapting neural responses.
source: Other studies have used predictive coding and efficient coding frameworks to construct models of adapting neural responses (Chopin and Mamassian, 2012; Młynarski and Hermundstad, 2018; May and Zhaoping, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to other studies

claim: The model incorporates a biologically plausible spike-frequency adaptation mechanism.
source: however, our model incorporates a biologically plausible spike-frequency adaptation mechanism.

claim: The potentially harmful effects of adaptation on individual neuron encoding can be mitigated by a coordinated population response.
source: Our study shows that the potentially harmful effects of adaptation on the individual neuron's ability to encode a stimulus can be mitigated by a coordinated population response.

claim: Other studies propose updating the decoder or divisive gain control mechanisms to address history-dependence caused by adaptation.
source: Other studies that have addressed this issue propose updating the decoder (Benucci et al., 2009) or have considered divisive gain control mechanisms (Schwartz et al., 2009) as well as synaptic plasticity mechanisms (Hosoya et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to other studies

claim: The study offers a framework for resolving the cost-accuracy tradeoff on a shorter time scale than the operating time scale for synaptic plasticity.
source: Our study offers an alternative, plausible framework for resolving the cost-accuracy tradeoff on a shorter time scale than the operating time scale for synaptic plasticity.
evidence: Comparison of the model to other approaches

claim: The model derives a prescription for voltage dynamics so that network neurons can produce a reconstruction of any stimulus with fixed decoder and recurrent weights.
source: we derive a prescription for the voltage dynamics so that the network neurons can produce a reconstruction of any stimulus with fixed decoder and recurrent weights.

claim: The model is developed from a normative encoding framework.
source: Our model is developed from a normative encoding framework (Boerlin et al., 2013; Druckmann and Chklovskii, 2012; Olshausen and Field, 1996; Spratling, 2010)
evidence: Description of the model foundation with citations

claim: The new contribution compared to Boerlin et al. (2013) is to allow more flexibility in the form that the metabolic cost can take.
source: The new contribution compared to Boerlin et al. (2013) is to allow more flexibility in the form that the metabolic cost can take.

claim: The time scales of the cost and of the representation are disassociated which leads to distinct dynamics for the cost and for the neural firing rate.
source: In particular, the time scales of the cost and of the representation are disassociated which leads to distinct dynamics for the cost and for the neural firing rate.

claim: The approach can be generalized to many other types of cost, arbitrary weights, and number of neurons.
source: This approach can be generalized to many other types of cost, arbitrary weights, and number of neurons.

claim: Diverse adaptation properties within a population can be an asset.
source: Our model suggests that diverse adaptation properties within a population can be an asset.

claim: The variability of adaptation effects has been observed in V1 neurons.
source: The variability of adaptation effects has been observed in V1 neurons (Jeyabalaratnam et al., 2013; Nemri et al., 2009; Ghisovan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: A heterogeneous population of neurons is able to better distribute the cost to maximize efficiency in different contexts.
source: A heterogeneous population of neurons is able to better distribute the cost to maximize efficiency in different contexts.

claim: Studies in the retina show that retinal ganglion cells with different adaptive properties complement each other.
source: Studies in the retina show that retinal ganglion cells with different adaptive properties complement each other such that sensitizing cells can improve the encoding of weak signals when fatiguing cells adapt (Kastner and Baccus, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kastner and Baccus, 2011

claim: Heterogeneities in adaptation contribute to complex dynamics in neural spike trains.
source: At the same time, these heterogeneities contribute to complex dynamics in the neural spike trains (Dragoi et al., 2000; Okun et al., 2015; Nirenberg et al., 2010; Mohar et al., 2013; Wissig and Kohn, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: The model predicts that neurophysiological studies may exhibit an experimental bias resulting in highly responsive neurons being overrepresented in the sample.
source: We make the prediction that neurophysiological studies where single neuron activity is recorded may exhibit an experimental bias that results in highly responsive neurons being overrepresented in the sample.

claim: The study challenges the notion that tuning is a static characteristic of neurons.
source: Moreover, our study challenges the notion that tuning is a static characteristic of neurons.

claim: Experiments increasingly reveal that neurons change their tuning dynamically with changing stimulus statistics.
source: Experiments increasingly reveal that neurons change their tuning dynamically with changing stimulus statistics (Hollmann et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2008; Hosoya et al., 2005; Nagel and Doupe, 2006; Smirnakis et al., 1997; Solomon and Kohn, 2014; Wark et al., 2007; Wark et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: In the visual cortex, the tilt after effect has the effect of shifting the tuning curves of neurons away from their preferred orientations.
source: In the visual cortex, it has been shown that the tilt after effect is not only an effect of response suppression but that it also has the effect of shifting the tuning curves of neurons away from their preferred orientations (Jin et al., 2005; Ghisovan et al., 2009; Dragoi et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: A great deal of tuning change may be a network effect rather than an intrinsic neuronal effect.
source: our study shows that a great deal of the change may be a network effect rather than an intrinsic neuronal effect.

claim: The extent of adaptation for a single neuron may be difficult to predict without considering the properties of the rest of the network.
source: Thus, the extent of adaptation for a single neuron may be difficult to predict without considering the properties of the rest of the network (Fairhall, 2014).
evidence: Conclusion from the model with supporting citation

claim: When the network is considered as a whole, the adaptive effects in one neuron can be compensated for by another neuron that reports to the same readout.
source: however, we show that when the network is considered as a whole, the adaptive effects in one neuron can be compensated for by another neuron that reports to the same readout.

claim: The apparently complex adaptation at the single neuron level is an indicator of the manner in which the signal is encoded by the network as a whole.
source: In other words, the apparently complex adaptation at the single neuron level is not an impediment to the network but rather an indicator of the manner in which the signal is encoded by the network as a whole.

claim: The model applies at the level of relatively densely connected, and thus local, populations.
source: Our model applies at the level of relatively densely connected, and thus local, populations.

claim: Observing the organized transfer of responses between neurons through adaptation and E/I balance would require recording a significant proportion of locally connected neurons.
source: Observing the organized transfer of responses between neurons through adaptation and E/I balance would require one to record a significant proportion of these neurons locally (neurons that are likely to be interconnected directly or through interneurons).

claim: Recent experimental techniques render such recordings possible.
source: Recent experimental techniques render such recordings possible (Buzsáki, 2004)

claim: There should exist a decoder of neural activity, independent of stimulus history, that can detect the stimulus despite large changes in neural activity over time.
source: First of all, there should exist a decoder of neural activity, independent of stimulus history that can detect the stimulus despite large changes in neural activity over time.
evidence: Prediction from the model for experimental validation

claim: Shuffling the neural responses between the early and latter part of responses to a prolonged stimulus should have detrimental effects on stable decoding.
source: Second of all, shuffling the neural responses, for example between the early and latter part of the responses to a prolonged stimulus, should have detrimental effects on such stable decoding.
evidence: Prediction from the model for experimental validation

claim: Over the course of adaptation, the activity of different neurons should not vary independently.
source: And finally, over the course of adaptation, the activity of the different neurons should not vary independently.
evidence: Prediction from the model for experimental validation

claim: Neural responses over time are constrained on a subspace where the stimulus representation is stable.
source: we might be able to observe that neural responses over time are constrained on a subspace where the stimulus representation is stable.
evidence: Prediction from the model for experimental validation
